Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60
[https://doi.org/10.1007/s10515-026-00607-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10515-026-00607-y)
## **Effort estimation in scrum using AI**

**Maria Rasheed** **[1]** **· Iman Fatima** **[1]** **· Darain Fatima** **[1]** **· Muhammad Hamid** **[1]** **·**
**Fahima Hajjej** **[2]**

Received: 4 June 2025 / Accepted: 14 February 2026
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature
2026

**Abstract**
Scrum, an agile methodology emphasizing iterative development and adaptive plan-­
ning, facilitates high-quality software delivery. However, achieving accurate effort
estimation (measured in story points) for Scrum projects is often challenged by fac-­
tors such as shifting requirements, varying task complexities, and inherent biases in
traditional estimation techniques. To address these limitations, this study proposes
and rigorously evaluates an ensemble Machine Learning (ML) model, integrating
Ridge Regression (RR), Extra Trees (ET), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The
model’s efficacy was confirmed through a multi-faceted evaluation. Firstly, on a
public dataset of 140 user stories, it achieved strong performance Mean Absolute
Error (MAE) of 0.68, Mean Square Error (MSE) of 0.74, Root Mean Square Error
(RMSE) of 0.86. This improvement was demonstrated to be statistically significant
(p < 0.05) via the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Secondly, to address the critical re-­
search gap of generalizability, the model’s robustness was validated on a secondary,
real-world dataset of 159 user stories, where it maintained its superior performance
(MAE=0.70, MSE=0.90, RMSE=0.95). Finally, a detailed error analysis provides
actionable insights for practitioners, linking the model’s performance to the agile
best practice of decomposing large user stories. The findings validate that the pro-­
posed ensemble model offers a statistically robust, generalizable, and practically
applicable data-driven solution for enhancing sprint planning and resource alloca-­
tion in agile project management.

**Keywords** Agile · Ensemble model · Effort estimation · Machine learning ·
Scrum · User story

**1 Introduction**


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


Software engineering refers to the process of creating software using structured
approaches and processes to meet scope, cost, time and quality requirements of
projects. Traditionally, the waterfall paradigm was used to develop projects, which
involves sequential phases of analysis, design, implementation, testing and deploy-­
ment (Hohl et al. 2018). However, this sequential lifecycle is inappropriate for mod-­
ern software development, as it requires an upfront definition of all requirements,
delays user feedback and provides little flexibility in meeting changing project
requirements. Recognizing these limitations, a new approach of software develop-­
ment based on the agile Manifesto, was introduced by a group of software experts
in 2001 (Hohl et al. 2018; Tawosi et al. 2022). Consequently, agile methodology has
become popular in the software development process because of flexible workflow, a
focus on fast information exchange, and iterative cycles (Tawosi et al. 2022). This is
an iterative method that enhances faster development, better quality output, and user
satisfaction via feedback and collaboration. Scrum is one of the most popular agile
methodologies employed in practice today. Scrum methodology provides a highly
structured yet flexible method of managing the development phases of the com-­
plex projects from inception to completion. Its fundamental principles are repeated
development of progress, flexibility to change, and strong collaboration, which is
specifically effective for projects with dynamic requirements (Sánchez et al. 2023).
In the scrum methodology, requirements are defined in form of user stories. These
user stories are organized and prioritized in the product backlog which is a dynamic
repository of all the work that should be completed. A user story itself is a concise,
non-technical description of a software requirement articulated from the end- user’s
perspective, typically adhering to the structure:“As a [user type], I want [goal] so that

[reason or benefit]”. Effort estimation is a critical phase in user story development
(Sánchez et al. 2023; Alsaadi and Saeedi 2024). In order to estimate the effort needed
to complete user stories, developers take into consideration a number of different fac-­
tors such as resource requirements and the complexity of user stories. Accurate effort
estimation, often measured in story points, is an essential part of agile software devel-­
opment because an inaccurate estimate can cause serious barriers to the project. The
estimation of effort can be divided into two methods: expert-based methods, relying
on the knowledge and past experience of the team members along with the project
data and the data-driven methods, which rely on historical information of similar
completed projects. This historical data includes information of user stories, related
subtasks, complexities, and overall rate of resource utilization, enabling predictive
models to estimate efforts in new projects (Alsaadi and Saeedi 2024). While team
members in Scrum estimate effort during sprint planning, traditional methods often
prove inadequate, leading to inaccuracies. These inefficiencies with the traditional
effort estimation pose a consistent problem in Scrum projects. Other causes of inac-­
curate estimates include the biases in human nature (e.g., optimism or pessimism),
the subjective estimates, and the inconsistent application of estimating techniques
across different teams or projects. These imprecise estimations of story points, which
are directly used to inform sprint scoping and commitment, may trigger serious
problems, such as poor sprint planning, inefficient resource allocation, inability to
# `1 3`


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


Page 3 of 24 60


achieve sprint goals, project overruns, and massive budget overruns. Such unreli-­
ability compromises one of the strengths of agile project management; its predictable
and incremental delivery of value (Tawosi et al. 2022; Chauhan et al. 2021). Thus,
one of the major issues in Scrum practice is the need of more precise, objective and
reliable approaches for the estimation of user story effort. To satisfy this need, the
trend shifted from expert-based approaches to data driven methods especially ML
(Sudarmaningtyas and Mohamed 2021). Initial work in this field typically used a
single model of ML (e.g., Decision Tree, SVR) on past data. Although these single
models were promising, they often had their own flaws, which included a high sensi-­
tivity to data distribution, a tendency to overfit, or a natural bias towards a particular
type of patterns (Alsaadi and Saeedi 2024). As a result, their generalizability to other
projects was frequently low. This study explores the use of an ensemble learning
method in order to address the limitations of these single models. The main idea of
an ensemble is to combine the predictions of different models so that the weaknesses
of one model can be counterbalanced by the strength of another. The objective of this
technique is to generate a single and stronger and highly generalizable model to make
effective effort estimations However, proposing a new model is not enough rather it
should be strictly tested to overcome the research gaps of statistical significance and
generalizability that were encountered in the earlier studies. To guide this rigorous
investigation, this study seeks to answer the following research questions:

- RQ1: To what extent can the proposed ensemble ML model accurately predict the
effort of user stories?

RQ2: Which effort drivers are the most influential in the model’s prediction pro-­
cess, and what is their relative importance?

To answer these questions systematically, the research contributions of the paper are
as follows:

1. Proposed a novel ensemble model that strategically integrates three methodolog-­

ically diverse ML models a regularized linear model (RR), a randomized treebased method (ETs), and a neural network (Multi-Layer Perceptron) to improve
predictive accuracy and robustness by mitigating the biases of individual models.
2. Added a level of statistical rigor by conducting the Wilcoxon signed-rank test

in order to statistically prove that the improvements in the performance of the
proposed model are statistically significant ( *p <* 0 *.* 05 ).
3. Fills in the key research gap of generalizability by conducting an intensive cross
dataset validation. The model was tested on a secondary and real-world dataset,
which indicated that it could preserve high performance in different setting and
indicated that it is practically applicable.
4. Provides practical, data driven insights to agile practitioners by connecting an in
depth analysis of errors with the agile best practice of breaking down large user
stories. This converts the findings of this model into useful recommendations of
enhancing the accuracy of estimation in the real-life sprint planning.
# `1 3`

Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents a literature review.
Section 3 provides a detailed description of the methodology. Section 4 contains
results and discussion and conclusion is given in Section 5.

**3 Methodology**

The methodology involves 5 primary stages 1) Data collection, 2) Data Preprocess-­
ing that transforms data into a form understandable by ML algorithms, 3) Feature
extraction, 4) Model development to estimate effort, and 5) Evaluations of the model.

**Fig. 1** Workflow of proposed Methodology for effort estimation in scrum

**3.1 Data collection**

The dataset used in this study is the User_stories_dataset (Alsaadi and Saeedi 2024),
which is a publicly available dataset found on Mendeley Data. It is a dataset of 140
instances representing a unique user story and its characteristics. For each user story,
the dataset offers 12 input features, usually known as effort drivers. These features
can be classified as follows:

**3.1.1 Numerical features (6)**

- **Team members:** The number of team members involved.

- **Experience:** The average experience of team members in months.

- **Size:** A numeric value indicating the size of the user story (1-5 with 1 indicating
small size and 5 indicating large size).

- **Complexity:** A numeric description of the complexity of the user story (1 to 5,
where 1 is low and 5 is high).

- **Priority:** A numerical value of the priority of the user story.

- **No of tasks:** The sub-tasks of the user story.

**3.1.2 Categorical features (6)**

- **PL:** The language (e.g. C#, Java, python, html).

- **Development type:** The type of development (e.g. ‘M’ Mobile, Hardware devel-­
opment, web, DL Model, database).

- **platform:** The target platform (e.g. ‘Android Studio, Unity, IOS, python, .net,
Google Colab, etc.).

- **External hardware:** A binary value (0 or 1) of external hardware need.

- **Related technologies:** Certain technologies used (e.g., ‘AR’, ‘Location’, ‘AI’,
# `1 3`


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


Page 7 of 24 60


‘IoT’, ‘Voice recognition’, ’Computer vision, ’Gamification, ’LBT, or 0, in case
not).

- **DBMS:** The database management system (e.g. ‘Unity’, ‘Vuforia’, ‘Firebase’,
‘none’, ‘SQL’, ‘Place note’).

The target variable is the effort. The measure of effort in this dataset is in story points.
These story points are numbered values that development teams use to measure how
much work they will have to do to implement a user story and which often have a
Fibonacci-like structure (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21).

**3.1.3 The cross-validation dataset (generalizability resource)**

In order to fill the critical research gap of model generalizability, a second, indepen-­
dent dataset was gathered and used to provide strong validation. This resource, a sig-­
nificant element of the generalizability analysis of this study, was obtained from 36
real-world software projects of professional software houses after a rigorous multistep process.

The data collection procedure was carried out in three phases:


1. **Identification of Effort Drivers:** 13 main effort drivers were identified using

two-fold methodology. An extensive Literature Review identified 12 general
factors related to Team (Experience, Team members), Story (Size, Complexity,
Priority, No of tasks), and Technical context (PL, Platform, DBMS, etc.). Impor-­
tantly, Industry Insights obtained through the consultation with Scrum Masters
and the assessment of the actual software projects revealed one more crucial
factor: ’Requirements Volatility’. The inclusion of this factor makes the dataset
more reflective of the actual risks in projects.
2. **Structured Data Compilation:** A structured and detailed questionnaire was

designed to capture the relevant data. This tool was used to gather data (in Fibo-­
nacci Story Points) of 160 user stories obtained through completed projects,
ensuring that the data were real development scenarios.
3. **Quality Assurance:** A systematic quality assurance process was used to ascer-­

tain the validity of the dataset. All user stories were assessed according to atomi-­
city, uniqueness and completeness requirements. Such a meticulous screening
has led to a curated list of 159 user stories which were used in cross-validation.

This secondary data is entirely different compared to the publicly available resource
(User stories dataset). It was not used to train the model. It is the source of the strong
Cross-Dataset Validation, which was conducted in Section 4.2, which provides evi-­
dence of the practical applicability and stability of the ensemble model in an unseen
environment.

**3.2 Data preprocessing**

Preprocessing of data is a very important step to convert raw data into a form that can
be used by the ML algorithm. Since this dataset has a number of categorical variables
# `1 3`


60 Page 8 of 24


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


(e.g., Platform, PL, Development type, DBMS, etc. listed in Section 3.1), they had
to be transformed into a numerical form. For this standard One-Hot Encoding (OHE)
was used (Samuels 2024). OHE is a popular method of transforming non- ordinal cat-­
egorical variables into a binary matrix format. In this process every distinct category
in a feature is converted into a new binary (0 or 1) feature. 1 means the presence of
that category of an instance and 0 means absence of it. This change causes ML mod-­
els not to make false inferences about an ordinal relationship between categories that
2
do not exist (e.g. falsely assuming that Android Studio > Unity). Figure is a demon-­
stration of one such standard encoding process on a hypothetical categorical feature.

**3.3 Feature selection**

One of the key steps to optimizing the performance of the model is feature selection,
in which the most relevant features (effort drivers) are selected and irrelevant features
are discarded. In this study, Mutual Information (MI) has been selected to evaluate
the importance of features and to control the selection process [18]. As compared
to simple correlation coefficients, which are mostly used to identify linear relation-­
ships, MI can be used to quantify both linear and non-linear associations between the
input features and the target variable (’effort, story points). This is especially critical,
because the factors affecting software effort tend to interact in complex, non-linear
fashion. MI is a measure of the quantity of information learned about a single vari-­
able (e.g., ‘effort’) by observing another variable (e.g., ‘complexity’), and is simply
a direct measure of the relevance of a feature. Greater MI scores are an indication

of stronger dependencies and consequently, more predictive power. This research
utilized the non-parametric MI estimation method proposed by Ross (2014), which
employs a KNN technique suitable for the mixed data types present in this data-­
set after one-hot encoding of categorical variables. The results of this analysis, per-­
formed strictly on the training data to prevent information leakage, are visualized in
Fig. 3. This graph presents the overall importance of each feature, with scores for
categorical variables aggregated for clarity. Based on this ranking, the top 5 features,
namely Complexity, Size, related technologies, PL, and platform, were selected for
model development.

**3.4 Model development**

To estimate the effort of agile user stories, an ensemble voting regressor model was
created, which combines multiple supervised ML algorithms trained on the data-­
set to overcome individual model’s limitations. The top-performing algorithms are
selected, and their results are averaged to produce the final estimation. The following
ML algorithms are used in this study.

**Fig. 2** An illustration of the One-Hot Encoding process applied to a categorical feature

**Fig. 3** Overall feature importance based on aggregated MI scores

**3.4.1 Ridge regression (RR)**


Page 9 of 24 60


RR is a regularized linear regression technique that incorporates an L2 penalty term


*α* [1]

2


*n*
∑

*i* =1


*θ* *i* [2] [ into the cost function, where ] *[α]* [ controls the regularization strength and ] *[θ]* *[i]*


represents the model coefficients. This penalty term shrinks the coefficients, reducing
their magnitude and mitigating overfitting, particularly in scenarios with high-dimen-­
sional or multicollinear data. RR achieves model generalization by balancing bias
and variance, which makes it ideal for effort estimation because robust and stable pre-­
dictions are vital to these tasks. The model performance can be enhanced by adjusting
the regularization parameter *α* for predicting accurate and credible efforts in software
development or project management contexts.

**3.4.2 Extra trees (ET)**

Extremely Randomized Trees is a tree-based ensemble learning technique, which is
similar to Random Forest, but with a higher degree of randomization in the splitting.
ET picks the thresholds randomly in the process of splitting and this gives it a balance
of high bias and low variance. With the adoption of this method, ET is able to train
quicker than the traditional Random Forest training methods. ET can be useful in the
effort estimation process since it constructs several decision trees that realize good
generalization across the user stories with effective computational efficiency.
# `1 3`


60 Page 10 of 24

**3.4.3 Decision tree (DT)**


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


The hierarchical model of DTS is used in the classification and regression functions.
The models spread data through decision points and have evaluation criteria includ-­
ing Gini impurity or entropy, thereby making them human-readable and intuitive.
These models exhibit distinct value in the effort estimation process since they exhibit
complicated associations between user story attributes and estimated work time. The
models are prone to overfitting, and this can be reduced through pruning algorithms
as well as rule constraints, which specify maximum depth.

**3.4.4 Random forest (RF)**

RF is a collection of DTs that introduces randomness in the process of enhancing
generalization. The method constructs many decision trees based on individual data
sets and then it applies input averaging to generate combined predictions. Random
Forest balances accuracy and overfitting through their implementation process. A
RF model manages several user stories by finding vital characteristics that define the
level of precision in estimations and contains story complexity and team experience
as the important factors.

**3.4.5 Support vector regressor (SVR)**

SVR functions as a regression model derived from Support Vector Machines (SVM)
for making predictions about continuous outputs. The approach creates prediction
areas that extend throughout the estimated value region by up to epsilon. The algo-­
rithm applies kernel functions (linear, polynomial, RBF) to raise data dimensions so
a linear regression model can operate effectively. Through kernel functions, SVR
establishes complex connections between project features and predicted effort values.

**3.4.6 K-Nearest neighbors (KNN)**

KNN is a non-parametric instance-based learning algorithm that predicts outcomes
based on the nearest training examples. It predicts based on the similarity (distance)
between data points. For a given data point, it finds the KNN in the training set. For
classification, it assigns the most common class among the neighbors. For regression,
it averages the values of the neighbors. The distance metric (e.g., Euclidean, Manhat-­
tan) determines how similarity is measured.

**3.4.7 Multi-layer perceptron (MLP)**

MLP is an artificial neural network that comprises multiple layers of neurons. It can
detect intricate data patterns related to the estimation of effort. The functions of acti-­
vation such as ReLU and backprop are used in MLPs. Within the context of user story
effort estimation, MLP is able to model complex feature-estimated effort relation-­
ships, and is useful when the decision boundaries are not readily determined using
tree-based models.
# `1 3`


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60

**3.4.8 Ensemble model**


Page 11 of 24 60


An ensemble model is a method of ML, which integrates the predictions of vari-­
ous single models to enhance the performance, the accuracy, and the resilience. It
combines the strengths of various models and reduces weaknesses of each of the
models leading to more reliable predictions. An ensemble model was also created
in this study by combining three ML algorithms, which include ET, RR and MLP.
The ensemble model combines the outputs of the individual models, and experimen-­
tal outcomes revealed that it performed better than individual models in estimating
efforts.

**3.4.9 Hyperparameter optimization**

A systematic process of hyperparameter tuning was implemented in order to maxi-­
mize the predictive performance of every model. The data were optimized by employ-­
ing a Grid Search strategy on the training sub-set of data. The aim of this procedure
was to determine the set of parameters that gave the lowest MAE of each algorithm.
Table 1 shows the final optimized parameters obtained after this process.

**3.5 Evaluation phase**


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


The final phase of the methodology is the evaluation of the model. For performance
evaluation, the dataset was partitioned into a training set and a testing set using a
fixed 80/20 split. Specifically, 80% of the data (112 instances) was randomly selected
for training the models, and the remaining 20% (28 instances) was held out for test-­
ing and evaluating their generalization performance. To ensure the randomness and
reproducibility of the split, a fixed random seed was used during the partitioning
process. The models were trained solely on the training set, and their predictive per-­
formance was then assessed on the unseen testing set using the evaluation metrics.
Different evaluation metrics exist for effort estimation. The evaluation metrics used
in this paper are described below.

**3.5.1 Mean absolute error (MAE)**

MAE (Qi et al. 2020) measures the average absolute differences between predicted
values and actual values. It is less sensitive to large errors than RMSE and provides a
straightforward interpretation of model error. MAE is optimal for models with Lapla-­
cian error distributions. The formula for MAE is:


MAE = [1]

Where n is the number of user stories, ActualEffort is the true value, and PredictedEf-­
fort is the value estimated by the model. Performance results using MAE for indi-­
vidual models with varying K feature selections are presented in Table 2.

**3.5.2 Mean squared error (MSE)**

MSE (Varshini and Kumari 2020) is a commonly used metric in regression analysis
to measure the average squared difference between the observed (actual) values and
the predicted values. It quantifies the accuracy of a predictive model by calculating
the average of the squared errors, where the error is the difference between the actual
and predicted values. The formula for MSE is:

**4 Results and discussion**

To provide meaningful comparison of Scrum effort estimation techniques, it is nec-­
essary to analyze not only the numerical accuracy, but also the ability of the meth-­
ods to demonstrate statistical reliability and generalizability. The estimation method
can only be considered dependable when their performance is tested on more than
# `1 3`


60 Page 14 of 24


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


a single dataset and supported by rigorous statistical testing. The discussion below
adheres to this principle, as it first establishes the performance of the proposed
model and then explains these results within the broader context of existing litera-­
ture. A comparative summary of the suggested ensemble approach with a several
major studies is presented in Table 5. The comparison does not limited to number
measures (MAE and RMSE); it also highlights that previous research had consid-­
ered Statistical Significance Testing and Generalizability Validation, two attributes
to fruitful empirical assertions. As demonstrated, the proposed model achieves the
best numerical results (MAE 0.68, RMSE 0.86). More importantly, the comparison
shows critical gaps in previous research. As an example, Shidiq et al. (2023) found
Gradient Boosting a good performer (MAE 0.90, RMSE 1.70), but no statistical test
was conducted, leaving the claims of improvement to chance. Similarly, Sánchez
et al. (2023) used Random Forest and AdaBoost with relatively good accuracy (MAE
0.81, RMSE 1.20), which admittedly were not as large because the dataset used is
relatively small, but again did not confirm that the improvements were significant.
Dave et al. (2021) introduced a Neuro-Fuzzy model (MAE 0.80, RMSE 1.23) but
the validation remained confined to single dataset, which limited the generalization.
Likewise, the ensemble model, developed by Alsaadi and Saeedi (2024) (MAE 0.78,
RMSE 1.15), was tested on a single public dataset, which undermines its flexibility
assertion.

These shortcomings are directly tackled by the proposed study. Through the inte-­
gration of the ET, RR and MLP with the validation of the ensemble using a Wilcoxon
signed-rank test and Cross-Dataset Validation, this piece of work provides a robust
and verifiable benchmark of Scrum effort estimation. A systematic feature selection
and model evaluation procedure was conducted to come up with the final ensemble.
Subsets of features with *k* = 3 to *k* = 12 were evaluated, and the relevance of the
features was ranked by MI. Each ML models, including ET, RR, MLP, KNN, Ran-­

dom Forest, Decision Tree and SVR, were tested on each features subset. Tables 2,
3, 4 give detailed results (MAE, MSE, RMSE) of all models and all feature counts.
Across these experiments, a consistent trend emerged there was a sub set of five
features that yielded the least error measures with most models. These five features
were Complexity, Size, related technologies, PL, and platform. The performance of
all individual learners is visualized in Fig. 4.

Considering this optimal five feature subset specifically, a further assessment of
each model revealed that RR was particularly successful with an MAE of 0.691,
MSE of 0.974 and RMSE of 0.974. Its strength is mostly due to stabilizing effect
of regularization, which serves to reduce overfitting. ET also performed well (MAE
0.705, MSE 1.004, RMSE 1.004), having the advantage of being built by randomly
selecting trees, and thus minimizing variance. MLP achieved MAE 0.735, MSE
1.719 and RMSE 1.719, which was competitive, but with a slightly higher error,
because of the sensitivity to network structure and data size. Other models (KNN,
RF, Decision Tree) gave higher values of error, and the SVR gave the highest errors,
probably because it uses hyperparameters that are highly tuned. According to this
analysis, RR, ET, and MLP were chosen as the most trustworthy candidates for the
ensemble. The ensemble was constructed then based on these three models that had
been trained specifically on the identified five-feature subset.

The ensemble had an MAE of 0.68, MSE of 0.74, and RMSE of 0.86 as indicated
in Table 6 and in Fig. 5. The wider view of all metrics and models performance is
# `1 3`


60 Page 16 of 24


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


**Fig. 5** Ensemble Model Vs Individual Models

presented with the help of line graphs in Table 6. Though these enhancements seem
noteworthy, the formal check of whether the differences are statistically significant
is necessary. The ensemble is strong due to the complementary nature of the com-­
ponents. RR offers a predictable linear base with high regularization; ET offers the
capability of modeling the nonlinear interaction but retains one with a low variance
and MLP offers the capacity to model complex and non-linear relationships in the
data. Their predictive errors are likely to counteract when combined, making more
stable and reliable estimations possible.

The selected features are also significant: Size and Complexity characterize the
intrinsic scale of the story, related technologies shows the team familiarity with the
technologies it needs, PL captures effects that are specific to a programming lan-­
guage, and platform affects the development environment. All these together make up
a powerful, interpretable, and informative set of features. Although the improvement
of the MAE between the best individual model (RR with 0.691) and the ensemble
model is relatively small, the significant decrease in MSE (0.974 to 0.74) and RMSE
(0.974 to 0.86) show that the ensemble suppresses larger errors better. This implies
that the ensemble does not only improve the average accuracy, but also improves
reliability by lowering the high-impact misestimations. The proposed approach pro-­
vides a better predictive ability in a variety of Scrum estimation problems through
its targeted feature selection, designed model combination, and regularization using
RR (Fig. 6).

**4.1 Statistical testing**

A formal statistical analysis was carried out to collect empirical evidence needed to
answer the research questions in the study. This section focus on RQ1, which chal-­
# `1 3`


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


Page 19 of 24 60

against Individual Components

lenges the level of the proposed ensemble model predictive accuracy and superior-­
ity. To overcome this, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was employed to compare the
paired prediction errors of the ensemble model with each of the three constituent
models; ET, RR, and MLP. The test was conducted on the held-out test set of 28
instances per pairing. Table 7 presents the results of these statistical comparisons and
serves as conclusive evidence on the performance of the model. The p-value in all
three comparisons is lower than the significant level of 0.05.

- The comparison with the RR ( *p* = 0 *.* 049 ), the most successful individual model,
demonstrates a near, but significant, advantage of the ensemble.

- The dominance is further increased as compared to ETs ( *p* = 0 *.* 029 ) and MultiLayer Perceptron ( *p* = 0 *.* 014 ), which has a lower baseline performance.

This consistent level of statistical significance of all components proves that the
improved performance of the ensemble model is not by chance. This gives good
statistical evidence to support the answer to RQ1 and confirm that the ensemble pro-­
posed is a valid and reliable addition to that of its constituent components. The main
hypothesis of RQ2 is also supported by the evidence as the capacity of the model to
deliver this higher performance is directly related to the effective implementation of
the most critical drivers of effort found in the research.

**4.2 Cross-dataset validation and generalizability analysis**

In order to resolve the pressing issue of model generalization, a cross-dataset valida-­
tion was carried out. The models that had been trained on small public data set of 140
user stories were tested on a new, more diversified real-world set of 159 user stories.
The aim of this rigorous test was to evaluate the capability of the models to perform
on totally unknown data in the new context. Table 8 summarizes the performance of
all the individual models and the proposed ensemble model on this new validation
dataset.
# `1 3`


60 Page 20 of 24


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


The findings of the cross-dataset validation, which are discussed in Table 8, are
strong arguments of the strength and high generalizability of the proposed ensem-­
ble model. The ensemble model again scored the least error rates in all metrics
( MAE = 0 *.* 70, RMSE = 0 *.* 95 ), clearly performing better than each of the individual
models on this new and unseen data, which confirm that it is effectiveness in not just
limited to a single dataset. One crucial observation can be made when comparing
these results to the original results on the 140-story dataset, where the performance
difference between the ensemble ( MAE = 0 *.* 68 ) and the optimal single model, RR
( MAE = 0 *.* 691 ) was extremely close. The performance of the single models dete-­
riorated on this new and more challenging real-world data more; e.g. the MAE of
the RR model increase to 0.76. Conversely, the ensemble model performance was
highly consistent and its MAE only slightly improved to 0.70 as illustrated in Fig. 7.
This fact is highly indicative of the fundamental assumption of ensemble model: the
individual models could work fine on the data that they were trained on, but they can
be fragile and ineffective when exposed to data of another distribution. By averaging
the predictions of a variety of models, the ensemble model manages to overcome
these individual weaknesses, smooth prediction errors, and achieve a high level of
accuracy, and is more resilient and generalizable.

The cross-dataset validation is a strong indication of the usefulness of the proposed
ensemble model in real-world situations. Its capability to sustain high performance
on an entirely different dataset confirms its potential to be a robust and generalizable
instrument in estimating effort utilized in real agile projects, directly mitigating the
major flaw of using models that were tested on one, small dataset.

**Fig. 7** MAE comparison of Model performance on Both datasets
# `1 3`


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60

**Fig. 8** Ensemble model error analysis across story complexity and size

**4.3 Error analysis**


Page 21 of 24 60


In order to get deeper insight into the performance and to understand the limitations
of the model, an error analysis was done in details. The purpose of this analysis was
to determine whether the errors in the model were systematically related to certain
features attributes. The MAE was compared at varying levels of the two most pow-­
erful features: ’Complexity’ and ’Size’. Graphical representation of the results in
Fig. 8(a) and (b) shows a very clear and stable trend. The mean prediction error is
insignificant when it comes to low-complexity, low-size user stories (levels 1 and 2),
which shows that there is an outstanding accuracy for standard, well-defined tasks.
However, the average error is most evidently growing with the increase of both the
complexity and size, and the maximum average errors were found between the most
complex and the largest user stories. This result implies that the proposed ensemble
model is most effective with most user stories, but its accuracy deteriorates slightly
when applied to unusually large and complex tasks. This is typical issue in effort
estimation, probably because such outlier stories are rarer in the training data, which
gives fewer examples to learn. This analysis confirms not only the robustness of
the model when dealing with typical and smaller user stories but also gives a clear
direction on the future work and practical implementation. One of the practical impli-­
cations of this finding is that this model is suitable in estimating effort of small to
medium sized user stories. The findings have solidly affirmed the agile best practice
of dividing large and complex user stories (epics) into smaller and manageable ones.
In this way, teams will be able to use this model to produce highly accurate estimates
of the effort of these smaller stories. The practice would not only make the sprint
planning more accurate but also consistent with the agile ideas of iterative develop-­
ment and reduction of risks.

**4.4 Answers to research questions**

This part reiterates the research questions that this paper set and gives answers
according to the empirical findings derived.
# `1 3`


60 Page 22 of 24


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


**RQ1: To what extent can the proposed ensemble ML model accurately predict the**
**effort of user stories?** **Answer:** The results indicate that the proposed ensemble
model has the ability to predict user story effort with a high level of accuracy. On the
main dataset, the model had a MAE of 0.68, a MSE of 0.74, and a RMSE of 0.86.
More importantly, it is not just numerically better than the individual constituent
models but statistically significant as well. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test, as described
in Statistical Testing (Section 4.1) was used to verify that improvement of the ensem-­
ble against the best of the individual models could be verified ( *p <* 0 *.* 05 ). Moreover,
the model was validated in terms of its robustness and generalizability with the help
of a strict cross-dataset validation. The discussions in Section 4.2 indicate that the

ensemble continued to be superior on an entirely novel, unseen dataset, which is
an important test of the practical viability of the ensemble. Altogether, these results
are a complete solution to RQ1: the ensemble method is the most appropriate to
resolve individual model biases and provides credible estimation instrument to use
with Scrum teams.

**RQ2: Which effort drivers are the most influential in the model’s prediction pro-­**
**cess?** **Answer:** The feature importance analysis, which is explained in Section 3.3
(Fig. 3), answers this question directly. The results showed that the most important
predictors of effort are Complexity and Size. These major drivers followed by related
technologies, PL and platform based on their relative influence on the predictions
of the model. The importance of the Complexity and Size is further supported by
the Error Analysis (Section 4.3). This comparison showed that the increase in these
two features is directly correlated with the increase in prediction error, and hence
these characteristics are predominant in predicting difficulty. This observation aligns
with the agile development principal, wherein the scope and complexity of a task are
thought to be the primary drivers of effort. The capability of defining these significant
drivers introduces transparency and assists teams to concentrate on the most impor-­
tant issues when planning sprints and discussing estimation.

**5 Conclusion and future work**

This study has successfully created, validated, and contextualize an ensemble learn-­
ing model to deal with the problem of inaccurate estimation of effort in Scrum proj-­
ects. The experiment showed that an integration of regularized linear model (RR),
randomized tree-based approach (ETs) and a neural network MLP can produce a
predictive model that is not only accurate but also statistically sound and practically
generalizable. The effectiveness of this method was confirmed by a multi- faceted
evidence-based process. The ensemble model had a good predictive performance
on the main public dataset of 140 user stories with a MAE of 0.68, MSE of 0.74
and RMSE of 0.86. This numerical superiority was subsequently statistically dem-­
onstrated to be statistically significant, which is an important step that had been
omitted in previous research. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test, indicated a substantial
advantage over not only the weaker constituent models ET ( *p* = 0 *.* 029 ) and MLP
( *p* = 0 *.* 014 ) but also the most successful individual model RR ( *p* = 0 *.* 049 ). More-­
# `1 3`


Automated Software Engineering      (2026) 33:60


Page 23 of 24 60


over, the critical research gap of generalizability was addressed directly in the study
by conducting a rigorous cross-dataset validation. The model was tested on a second,
real-world data of 159 user stories and it was found to retain its high quality per-­
formance ( MAE = 0 *.* 70, MSE = 0 *.* 90, RMSE = 0 *.* 95 ), significantly beating all the
other single models whose performance was deteriorated in new context. Lastly, the
study offered practical recommendations to practitioners by connecting an in-depth
analysis of errors to the agile best practice of breaking large user stories, thus taking
the empirical results of the model and applying them practically to real-life sprint
planning. Therefore, the study provides a full-end-to-end contribution in the sense
that it proposes a new algorithm and then thoroughly statistically validates it, tests its
generalizability, and presents an actual application of the new algorithm as a reliable,
validated, and powerful tool that Scrum teams can use to enhance their effectiveness
in managing projects. Based on this solid foundation, the future work will be aimed
at incorporating more developed Al methods. The next logical step is to consider
the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models
(LLMs) to derive deep semantic elements directly out of the textual descriptions of
the user stories.
